meta.subtitle: Off-price retail compounder: fiscal Q2 2027 net sales up 5% and a higher pre-tax margin, on a net-cash balance sheet

analystCommentary: We rate The TJX Companies BUY with a target range of $150 to $180, against a current price of $131.59. The second quarter of fiscal 2027 — the thirteen weeks ended August 1, 2026 — showed net sales of {+ $15.2 billion +}, {+ up 5% +} from $14.4 billion, on a {+ 4% +} increase in consolidated comp sales, and diluted EPS of {+ $1.36 +} versus $1.10. Part of the quarter's margin lift is non-recurring: TJX recognized a $219 million net benefit from IEEPA tariff refunds and has not booked a receivable for further refunds. Underneath the quarter is a durable off-price model — over 5,200 stores, prices generally 20% to 60% below full-price retailers, and a raised long-term store target. The balance sheet is net cash, and the company kept returning capital to shareholders during the quarter. The shares trade near the low end of their 52-week range, and the consensus target sits well above today's price, with most covering analysts rating the stock Buy. Our Base case is set below consensus to respect the non-recurring share of recent margin gains.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: The TJX Companies, Inc. operates as an off-price apparel and home fashions retailer worldwide, selling a rapidly changing assortment at prices generally 20% to 60% below full-price retailers' regular prices on comparable merchandise. The company was incorporated in 1962 and is headquartered in Framingham, Massachusetts. It runs over 5,200 stores through four segments: Marmaxx (TJ Maxx, Marshalls and Sierra in the U.S.), HomeGoods (HomeGoods and Homesense in the U.S.), TJX Canada (Winners, HomeSense and Marshalls), and TJX International (TK Maxx and Homesense in Europe and TK Maxx in Australia), alongside six e-commerce sites that together account for roughly 2% of sales. Revenue reached $60.4 billion in FY26, {+ up 7.1% +}, with net income of $5.5 billion and diluted EPS of $4.87. The vendor data treats TJX as a single consolidated reporting segment, so this report references the four operating segments qualitatively rather than by a numeric split.

thesis.body: TJX compounds sales through comparable-store growth and steady unit expansion, and converts that into rising cash returns. Consolidated comp sales rose {+ 4% +} in the second quarter of fiscal 2027 and {+ 5% +} across the six months ended August 1, 2026, driven by a higher average basket and more customer transactions, with home outpacing apparel. The off-price model gives the buying organization flexibility to source opportunistically and, per management, to mitigate tariff pressure. Gross margin has widened over recent years and the pre-tax margin expanded again in the latest quarter. A net-cash balance sheet funds both store growth toward the raised store target and continued FY26 shareholder returns. The counter-case: part of the recent margin gain came from a one-time tariff-refund benefit, the shares already sit below their 52-week high, and e-commerce remains a small part of a primarily brick-and-mortar business.

catalysts: Additional IEEPA tariff refunds: TJX has paid approximately $490 million in IEEPA-related tariffs and received $331 million of refunds in the second quarter of fiscal 2027, but has booked no receivable for the remainder, leaving potential upside if further phases are realized.

Comp-sales momentum and unit growth: mid-single-digit comparable-sales gains, with store count and selling square footage each up about 3% year over year, could extend the top line as TJX expands toward its raised store target.

Capital returns: TJX kept returning cash to shareholders through dividends and buybacks in the second quarter of fiscal 2027, and the net-cash balance sheet leaves room to sustain the payout and repurchases.
Re-rating toward the street: the consensus target implies substantial upside from the current price, and the analyst rating skew is heavily to Buy with none at Sell.
risks: Tariff and refund uncertainty: the tariff-refund benefit that lifted the quarter's margin is non-recurring, and the amount of any further IEEPA refunds is uncertain and may not match what TJX has already paid.
Competition and channel shift: TJX competes with larger, better-resourced retailers, and consumer e-commerce spending continues to rise while the business is primarily brick-and-mortar.
Merchant execution and inventory: the opportunistic buying model depends on merchants sourcing the right goods at the right prices, and misjudged demand can force markdowns.
Foreign currency: currency was a 1% drag on second-quarter fiscal 2027 net sales, and translation swings affect reported foreign-segment results.

financials.incomeCommentary: For the second quarter of fiscal 2027 — the thirteen weeks ended August 1, 2026 — net sales were $15.2 billion, {+ up 5% +} from $14.4 billion in the prior-year quarter, on a {+ 4% +} rise in consolidated comp sales. Diluted EPS was {+ $1.36 +} versus $1.10 a year earlier. The pre-tax profit margin was {+ 13.3% +}, {+ up 1.9 percentage points +} from 11.4%. The cost-of-sales ratio, including buying and occupancy costs, was 66.6%, {+ down 2.7 percentage points +} from 69.3%, helped by a net tariff-refund benefit and favorable merchandise markon; the SG&A ratio was 20.3%, {- up 0.8 percentage points -} from 19.5% on tariff-related compensation accruals and higher store wages. The vendor found no clean GAAP operating-income line, so operating margin is not meaningful; profitability is best read through the pre-tax margin and these ratios. Zooming out, revenue grew from $48.6 billion in FY22 to $60.4 billion in FY26, gross margin widened from 28.5% to 31.0%, and net income rose from $3.3 billion to $5.5 billion with diluted EPS of $4.87. Consensus looks for about $64 billion of revenue and $5.33 of EPS in FY27E and $68 billion and $5.79 in FY28E.
financials.balanceCommentary: TJX carries a net-cash position. Net debt was {+ -$3.4 billion +} in FY26, more net cash than the -$2.9 billion of FY22, though the balance did not build steadily — it narrowed to -$2.1 billion in FY23 before rebuilding to the FY26 level. Total debt was $2.9 billion and cash and short-term investments $6.2 billion. Total equity has grown steadily from $6.0 billion in FY22 to $10.2 billion in FY26. Liquidity is adequate but has eased: the current ratio was 1.14 in FY26 and 1.15 on a trailing-twelve-month basis, down from 1.27 in FY22. Consolidated average per-store inventories were up 2% at the end of the quarter, consistent with the lean-inventory model. The net-cash balance sheet gives management room to fund store growth and shareholder returns without leaning on debt.
financials.cashflowCommentary: Cash generation has strengthened. Operating cash flow rose from $3.1 billion in FY22 to $6.9 billion in FY26, and free cash flow reached $4.9 billion, an 8.1% FCF margin. Capital expenditure was $2.0 billion in FY26, funding store expansion and infrastructure. The company returned cash steadily: FY26 share repurchases were $2.5 billion and dividends $1.8 billion. With free cash flow comfortably covering the dividend and a net-cash balance sheet behind it, the buyback and dividend look well supported.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: TJX trades at 24.4x trailing earnings and 2.3x sales, with a forward P/E of 24.7x on next-twelve-month estimates and about 22.7x on FY28E EPS of $5.79. An EV/EBITDA multiple is not available because the vendor found no clean operating-income or EBITDA line. The shares are near the low end of a $122.78 to $170.00 52-week range at $131.59. The street is constructive: 18 of 22 analysts rate the stock Buy and none Sell, with a consensus target of $169.80 (+29.0%), a median of $175.00, and a range of $136.00 to $198.00. The dividend yields 1.47%. Peer multiples are not in the data set, so we assess the valuation on the company's own history and growth rather than against named competitors; the trailing multiple reflects the model's mid-single-digit revenue growth and expanding margins.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Comp sales stay mid-single-digit and unit growth advances toward the raised store target; merchandise markon stays favorable and further IEEPA refunds are realized; revenue and EPS track toward the upper end of the consensus estimate path, and the multiple re-rates toward the high end of the analyst target range.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Mid-single-digit comp and revenue growth in line with the FY27E consensus of about $64 billion and FY28E of $68 billion; the pre-tax margin holds near the low-13% area once the one-time tariff benefit lapses; the shares re-rate modestly but stay below the consensus target.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Comp sales decelerate, favorable merchandise markon reverses, and SG&A wage pressure and foreign-currency drag weigh on margin; further IEEPA refunds fall short of what TJX has paid; the multiple compresses toward and below the 52-week low.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: Our scenarios weight a 45% Base, a 30% Bull and a 25% Bear. The Base at $158 sits above today's price but below the consensus target, reflecting a normalization of margin once the one-time tariff-refund benefit lapses. The Bull at $185 assumes continued comp momentum, store growth toward the raised target and additional tariff refunds. The Bear at $108 sits below the 52-week low and assumes comp deceleration, margin give-back and shortfalls on further refunds, more than 15% under the current price. The probability-weighted fair value lands above today's price but short of consensus, and the reward-to-risk is favorable rather than lopsided — enough to support a BUY. Our Base and the low end of the range stay below consensus, while the $180 top of the range allows modest upside beyond it.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: The vendor reports TJX as a single consolidated segment; the company itself operates through four segments. Marmaxx runs TJ Maxx and Marshalls, plus tjmaxx.com and marshalls.com, in the United States, with Sierra reported within it. HomeGoods runs the HomeGoods and Homesense banners in the U.S. TJX Canada operates Winners, HomeSense and Marshalls in Canada. TJX International operates TK Maxx and Homesense in Europe and TK Maxx in Australia. Management has raised its long-term global store target, adding to the Marmaxx and HomeGoods store goals, and the home category outpaced apparel in comp-sales growth in the second quarter of fiscal 2027. Foreign-segment results are translated into U.S. dollars, so currency movements affect the consolidated figures.

moatFactors.name: Scale in opportunistic buying
moatFactors.body: TJX runs a large buying organization across more than 5,200 stores and four segments, giving it access to a broad flow of brand-name merchandise. Management states this sourcing model has helped mitigate tariff pressure, a scale advantage that smaller off-price competitors struggle to match.

moatFactors.name: Value gap
moatFactors.body: TJX sells generally at 20% to 60% below full-price retailers' regular prices on comparable merchandise, a value proposition that has supported comp-sales growth and a steadily widening gross margin over recent years.

moatFactors.name: Flexible, lean-inventory model
moatFactors.body: Lean inventory, frequent turns and a treasure-hunt assortment let TJX expand and contract categories as tastes shift; per-store inventories were up just 2% at the end of the second quarter of fiscal 2027 even as sales grew 5%.

moatFactors.name: Banner and geographic breadth
moatFactors.body: Multiple banners across the U.S., Canada, Europe and Australia diversify demand and real-estate opportunity, though this also exposes results to foreign-currency translation.

businessMoat.durability: The off-price model has proven durable: steady revenue growth across FY22 to FY26, a gross margin that has climbed over the same span, and comp-sales gains driven by more transactions rather than price alone. Scale in buying and a persistent value gap are hard for smaller rivals to replicate. The counter-case is real. TJX competes with larger, better-resourced retailers, some of which can source certain categories more consistently or invest faster in technology, including artificial intelligence. Consumer e-commerce spending continues to rise while TJX remains primarily brick-and-mortar, with online sales only a small share of the total. The model also depends on merchants judging demand correctly; misallocated inventory can force markdowns. On balance the moat is wide but must be continually re-earned through buying execution.

points: Comparable-store sales advanced 4% in fiscal Q2 2027 and 5% year-to-date, with the gains coming from more customer transactions and a higher average basket; home merchandise outpaced apparel.

Unit growth continues: store count and selling square footage each rose about 3% year over year, and the long-term global store target was raised to 7,500, with Marmaxx and HomeGoods targets up 300 and 200 stores.
Revenue grew again in FY26, and consensus looks for about $64 billion in FY27E (+6%) and $68 billion in FY28E.
Margin expansion: the pre-tax profit margin rose again in the second quarter of fiscal 2027, and the gross margin has continued to widen over recent years.
E-commerce remains roughly 2% of sales across six sites, a small base that is both a limited near-term contributor and longer-term optionality.

management.leadership: TJX is led by Ernie Herrman, Chief Executive Officer and President, with John Klinger as Senior Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer and Carol Meyrowitz as Executive Chairman. Douglas Mizzi and Kenneth Canestrari serve as Senior Executive Vice Presidents and Group Presidents. The proxy emphasizes that each named executive has decades of experience with the off-price business and that the board is focused on management continuity and succession planning. That depth of tenure is a strength for a model that depends on merchant judgment, though it also concentrates institutional knowledge in a long-serving team.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation balances reinvestment and returns. TJX converts strong operating cash flow into free cash flow well above its capital spending, and in FY26 it returned $4.3 billion to shareholders through dividends and buybacks, split between repurchases and a rising dividend. In the second quarter of fiscal 2027 it returned a further $1.3 billion. The dividend is comfortably covered by free cash flow, and the net-cash balance sheet lets the company invest toward its raised store target without financial strain. The main critique is that buybacks near a full valuation are less accretive than at lower prices.
management.governance: The DEF 14A dated April 2026 shows a Corporate Governance Committee that reviews and approves related-person transactions. The proxy discloses that several relatives of insiders are employed by TJX at compensation the proxy describes as consistent with other Associates at their levels and responsibilities: two adult children of Peter Benjamin ($228,282 and $148,979), an adult child and the spouse of an adult child of Kenneth Canestrari ($238,763 and $305,821), and an adult child of Carol Meyrowitz ($424,320). Shareholder support for pay has been strong, with 94% of votes cast in favor of say-on-pay in 2025, and incentive payouts were tied 100% to objective financial goals. The excerpt provided does not detail board composition, director independence or insider ownership, so those cannot be assessed here.

idiosyncratic: Tariff-refund realization: the net tariff-refund benefit recognized this quarter is stated after a $112 million offset for related compensation accruals, and TJX has recognized no receivable for potential further refunds; the total of any additional refunds is uncertain and may fall short of what the company has already paid in IEEPA-related tariffs.

Merchant execution and inventory: the opportunistic buying model places wide discretion with merchants; if they misjudge demand or fail to secure goods at sufficiently low prices, sales and margins can suffer and excess inventory can force markdowns.
Channel and competition: consumer e-commerce spending continues to rise while TJX is primarily brick-and-mortar with e-commerce near 2% of sales, and some competitors are larger and better-resourced.
Foreign currency: currency was a 1% drag on second-quarter fiscal 2027 net sales, and translation of TJX Canada and TJX International can meaningfully swing reported results.
risks.systemic: TJX's results depend on discretionary consumer spending, which is sensitive to the broader economy, employment and inflation. Management flags that tariffs on imports from China and other countries have caused significant volatility in the global economy and that the extent and duration of tariffs — and their effect on import costs, vendor and competitor pricing, consumer demand and retaliatory measures — remain uncertain. A U.S. Supreme Court decision in February 2026 invalidated the IEEPA tariffs, but the refund process is phased and incomplete. Currency movements and global supply-chain disruptions are additional macro factors outside the company's control.

body: We rate TJX BUY with a target range of $150 to $180 against the current $131.59: our Base at $158 and the low end of the range sit below the consensus target, while the $180 top allows modest upside beyond it. The off-price model keeps compounding — net sales, comp sales and diluted EPS all rose in the second quarter of fiscal 2027 — on a net-cash balance sheet that funds both store growth toward the raised target and the FY26 shareholder returns noted above.

The call is tempered rather than aggressive. Part of the quarter's margin lift was the one-time tariff-refund benefit, the SG&A ratio rose, and the shares sit closer to their 52-week low than their high, which argues both for value and for some market caution. That Base stays below the street, and the Bear at $108 is a genuine downside, but the probability-weighted outcome and reward-to-risk still favor ownership.
